clue.text: Untaxed dealings in coal or jet?

definitions.note: whimsical: a trade whose goods are all pitch-dark

blocks.note: first meaning: the hidden cash trade that escapes the taxman
second meaning, taken literally: commerce in goods that are byword examples of the darkest colour

explanation.surface: A shady trader sells coal and jet without paying any tax.
explanation.walkthrough: Coal and jet are both proverbially as dark as can be, so a market in them is literally a trade in that colour; the question mark flags the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names the hidden, untaxed sector where work is paid in cash and never declared to the revenue.

clue.text: Cricketers, each arriving at London Bridge …

blocks.note: batters are the players who bat in cricket
ea. is the standard abbreviation for each

explanation.surface: A cricket team, one by one, turns up at a bridge in London.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs on into the next clue, but this clue stands alone. BATTERSEA Bridge crosses the Thames in south-west London.
explanation.definitionFit: Battersea Bridge is one of the crossings over the Thames, so the name serves as an example of a capital's river crossing.

clue.text: … the match they’ve all travelled for

definitions.text: the match they’ve all travelled for

blocks.clueFragment: the match they’ve all travelled for
blocks.note: surface reading: following on from the cricketers arriving in London, the fixture the visiting team journeyed to play
setter's reading: any fixture played at the opponents' ground, which the visitors must journey to reach

explanation.surface: Continuing from the previous clue, the cricketers have come to London for a particular match.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links the two clues into one story, but this answer is simply the general term for a fixture on the other side's ground.
explanation.definitionFit: A fixture played at the opponents' venue requires the visiting side to journey there, unlike one at their own ground.

clue.text: The ultimate in snack foods for poet

indicators.note: the ultimate is the final one, so only the closing letter of the next word is used

blocks.note: the final letter of snack
eats is informal for food

explanation.surface: The finest snacks are prepared for a poet.
explanation.definitionFit: John Keats was an English Romantic poet, author of famous odes; the answer is an example of the category.

clue.text: Stupidly select old bayonet

indicators.note: something done stupidly is done without order or sense, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone foolishly picks an outdated bayonet.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means bladed weapons such as swords and bayonets, as opposed to firearms, so a bayonet is an instance.

clue.text: Almost noon: too soon

blocks.note: N is an abbreviation for noon
arriving too soon is being early

explanation.surface: It is nearly midday, which is too soon for something.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are adverbs meaning very close to but not quite, a straightforward synonym pairing.

clue.text: Bitcoin creator who works underground

blocks.note: first meaning: a computer that verifies transactions and so generates new cryptocurrency
second meaning: a worker at a pit or mine

explanation.walkthrough: Bitcoin creator suggests the currency's mysterious inventor, but it means anyone running the computing that mints new coins.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a pit worker digging coal and someone whose computers generate cryptocurrency by solving puzzles.

clue.text: Having lost uniform, one chasing ship’s officer

indicators.note: having lost something means it is no longer there, so a letter is taken out

blocks.note: someone chasing is a pursuer
U is uniform in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A chaser has shed their uniform and is after a ship's officer.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the U out of PURSUER to leave PURSER.
explanation.definitionFit: A purser is the officer on a vessel responsible for accounts, money and passengers' welfare.

clue.text: Get up, when music finally reaches conclusion

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the word before it

blocks.note: as can mean when, as in 'as I left'
the final letter of music
a conclusion is an end; reaches just places it after

explanation.surface: Someone stands up when the music comes to its close.
explanation.definitionFit: To get up, in the sense of climb or rise, is to move upwards, which the answer verb expresses.

clue.text: This marine is a blue

blocks.note: surface reading: a sea creature or soldier who is a blue, perhaps a sportsman
setter's reading: put the answer in front of the word marine and the compound is the name of a deep blue pigment

explanation.surface: A particular sea-going soldier is described as a blue.
explanation.walkthrough: This stands for the answer itself: ULTRA followed by marine makes ultramarine, a bright blue pigment.
explanation.definitionFit: Ultramarine is a vivid blue colour originally made from lapis lazuli, so the prefix plus marine names a blue.

clue.text: No sinners in this parish church?

definitions.text: No sinners in this parish church?

blocks.clueFragment: No sinners in this parish church?
blocks.note: surface reading: a church whose congregation is entirely virtuous
setter's reading: a common dedication for parish churches, which taken literally means every member is holy

explanation.surface: A wry wonder whether a local church contains nobody who has sinned.
explanation.walkthrough: Many English churches are dedicated to every holy figure at once; read literally, such a congregation would hold no sinners.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a common church dedication honouring every holy person, used as the name of many parish churches.

clue.text: Small surfaces where one sees runners and riders

definitions.text: where one sees runners and riders
definitions.note: a descriptive phrase standing for the plural noun

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small
ledges are narrow flat surfaces

explanation.surface: Narrow surfaces where people watch horses and jockeys, as at a racecourse.
explanation.walkthrough: Runners and riders is racing talk, but sledges have runners underneath and riders on top.
explanation.definitionFit: A sledge glides on two runners, its blades, and carries riders, so on these vehicles both are visible.

clue.text: Take place in powerful movement to spend lavishly

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: a surge is a sudden powerful rush forward
Pl. is the abbreviation for place in addresses

explanation.surface: A strong onrush happens, leading to extravagant spending.
explanation.walkthrough: Pl. is the street-address abbreviation for Place; 'Take' reads like an ordinary verb but tells the rush word to hold it.
explanation.definitionFit: To splurge is to spend money freely and extravagantly, often on a treat.

clue.text: More crazy, previously got up in pink

blocks.note: rose is the past tense of rise, to get up
madder is the comparative of mad

explanation.surface: Someone went crazier after rising, flushing pink.
explanation.walkthrough: Previously says the 'got up' word comes before the 'more crazy' one, reversing the clue's order.
explanation.definitionFit: Rose madder is a pinkish-red pigment made from the madder plant, used by painters.

clue.text: Where were slaves kept once? Antarctica?

blocks.note: first meaning: the southern US states where plantation slavery was centred
second meaning, taken literally: the far southern end of the globe

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase names a region of the United States, but read literally it fits the continent at the bottom of the world; the question mark flags that playful reading.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the usual name for the American states of the old plantation economy, and literally describes the polar continent.

clue.text: Showed we went in Boots

indicators.note: went means departed, so those letters leave the word

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written: these letters are the ones that leave

explanation.surface: We turned up at the Boots chemist shop.
explanation.walkthrough: Boots is a British high-street chemist chain, which the capital B suggests; here it means footwear. Remove WE from SHOWED.
explanation.definitionFit: To be shod is to be wearing footwear, so someone in boots fits the adjective.

clue.text: Whole lane out of order for a spooky time

indicators.note: things out of order are in the wrong sequence and must be rearranged

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An entire street is closed for a scary occasion.
explanation.definitionFit: The festival on 31 October is associated with ghosts, witches and costumes, making it an eerie season.

clue.text: A bit of spine needed by European in green underwear

indicators.note: in places one item within the phrase that follows

blocks.note: vert is green in heraldry
a bra is an undergarment
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A spinal part is required by a European wearing green undies.
explanation.walkthrough: Heraldry uses French colour names, so green is vert; the European sits between the colour and the underwear.
explanation.definitionFit: A vertebra is one of the small bones making up the backbone, so it is a piece of it.

clue.text: Work a large gemstone

blocks.note: op. (opus) is a work, especially of music
taken as written
L is the abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: Someone works on a big gem.
explanation.definitionFit: Opal is an iridescent mineral prized in jewellery, an example of a precious stone.

clue.text: Secret business taken up by religious sect

indicators.note: in a down entry, taken up means read from bottom to top

blocks.note: Co. is the abbreviation for company, a business
a cult is a small religious group

explanation.surface: A clandestine company is adopted by a sect.
explanation.definitionFit: Occult means hidden or esoteric, knowledge kept from ordinary people, matching the adjective for undisclosed.

clue.text: Rich congratulations for hooker

blocks.note: first meaning: wealthy
second meaning: praise shouted at a rugby hooker, whose job is to heel the ball back in the scrum

explanation.walkthrough: Hooker suggests something seedy, but in rugby the hooker hooks the ball backwards with a heel at the scrum, so the praise is a cheer for a good strike.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone wealthy, originally having good shoes, and here also cheers a scrum player's footwork.

clue.text: Hate exam, after two low grades

blocks.note: D and E are low marks in an exam grading scale
a test is an exam

explanation.surface: Someone loathes exams after getting two poor marks.
explanation.walkthrough: After puts the exam word behind the two grades.
explanation.definitionFit: Both verbs mean to dislike intensely, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Surface film made from a paint

indicators.note: something made from materials is built anew out of them, so the letters are reworked

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A thin coating has been produced using paint.
explanation.definitionFit: A patina is the thin layer, such as verdigris, that forms on metal or wood over time.

clue.text: Shortly arrive to approve navigator’s equipment

indicators.note: shortly means in brief form, so the word is cut short by its last letter

blocks.note: to arrive is to come
to pass a proposal is to approve it

explanation.surface: Arriving soon to sign off on a navigator's kit.
explanation.definitionFit: A magnetic direction-finder is the instrument a navigator uses to find north and steer a course.

clue.text: Endless unhappiness for skinflint

indicators.note: endless means without its end, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: misery is deep unhappiness

explanation.surface: A tightwad suffers never-ending sorrow.
explanation.definitionFit: A skinflint hoards money and hates spending, exactly the character of a miser.

clue.text: Remote branch not popular appointment

blocks.note: out is the opposite of in, meaning fashionable or popular
a post is a job or appointment

explanation.surface: A distant office of a firm is an unpopular posting.
explanation.definitionFit: An outpost is a distant settlement or station, like a far-flung office of an organisation.

clue.text: The last in a series of home games

indicators.note: of here means made out of, so the letters come from within the next words

blocks.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: The final fixture in a run of matches at home.
explanation.definitionFit: Omega is the final letter of the Greek alphabet, hence the end of any sequence.

clue.text: In weariness putting lust aside for a change

indicators.note: making a change means altering things, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone tired sets their desire aside to try something different.
explanation.walkthrough: Putting looks like part of the instruction but is filler joining the pieces; the letters of lust plus aside are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Lassitude is physical or mental tiredness and lack of energy, a near-synonym.

clue.text: Makes tea, mentioning the after-effect of punch

indicators.note: mentioning means saying something out loud, so the word is judged by its sound

blocks.note: a punch leaves a mark on the skin

explanation.surface: Someone makes tea while talking about the results of a blow.
explanation.walkthrough: Punch suggests the drink, which tea fits, but it is a blow.
explanation.definitionFit: To brew is to steep tea leaves in hot water, so the verb matches making a pot.

clue.text: Feel relieved, brewing herb tea at home on stove

indicators.note: brewing means mixing and steeping, so the following letters are stirred into a new order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged
an Aga is a British brand of range cooker
being in means at home

explanation.surface: Someone relaxes making herbal tea on the kitchen range.
explanation.walkthrough: On means placed after in an across clue, so the at-home piece follows the stove. An Aga is a heavy cast-iron range cooker common in British country kitchens.
explanation.definitionFit: To breathe again is an idiom for relaxing once a worry or danger has passed.
